title: Spinoza's calm
hookLine: Spinoza, not a Stoic, also taught that understanding our emotions' causes makes us freer (Ethics 5)

lines: NOT A STOIC, BUT CLOSE BY.
cards: Holland, the 1660s. A man sits at a bench grinding glass lenses for microscopes and telescopes, slow work, where a rushed hand ruins the piece.
Alongside the lenses, he is writing a book laid out like a geometry textbook: definitions, axioms, propositions, proofs.

It's about God, nature and the human mind, and its last part is about something very ordinary: how to be a little less pushed around by your own feelings. His name is Baruch Spinoza. He wasn't a Stoic, and he said so.
But today he sits on the porch's front step.

teach.b: First, the book. Spinoza's Ethics was published in 1677, the year he died. Its fourth part is titled, in the old English translations, Of Human Bondage: being dragged along by passions you don't understand.
The fifth part is about freedom. Second, the idea.
Early in part five, Spinoza argues that a feeling which is a passion, something that just happens to us, stops being a passion once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.

teach.h: SEE A FEELING'S CAUSE, IT LOOSENS.
teach.b: Put plainly: understand a feeling's causes, and it has less hold on you. Not because you crushed it, but because you saw it.
Anger at your sister turns out to be tiredness, an old childhood hurt and a missed lunch, all at once. Seen whole, it shrinks to its real size. Third, where he parts from the Stoics.

In the preface to that same part, Spinoza names them. The Stoics, he says, thought our feelings depend entirely on our will, so we could command them completely, though even they had to admit it takes long practice.
For Spinoza, the will alone isn't the tool.

teach.h: CURIOSITY IS A KIND OF DISTANCE.
teach.b: So he's a neighbor, not a member: close to Epictetus's idea that our judgments disturb us, but built on different ground.
Fourth, why it helps on a Tuesday. You can't always change a feeling by deciding to. But you can almost always get curious about it.
Curiosity is a kind of distance, and a little distance is a kind of freedom.

how: Readers of Spinoza often treat a strong emotion as something to understand rather than fight, tracing its causes until it loosens its grip.

o: a feeling ignored until it fades away
a feeling crushed by sheer force of will
a feeling understood, so it loosens its hold

s: Spinoza agreed with the Stoics that will alone can command our feelings
in the preface to part five he says they thought so, and that even they had to admit long practice was needed.
Spinoza's Ethics is laid out like a geometry book
he wasn't one, and named the Stoics as people he disagreed with.

games.q: you're furious and can't talk yourself out of it. what would Spinoza try?
o: trace where the anger came from
games.why: for Spinoza, a feeling understood through its causes loses its hold on us; understanding, not willpower, is the tool.

practice: Pick one feeling that's been with you today, irritation, worry, a low hum of sadness, and name it without trying to get rid of it.
Ask slowly where it came from, and let a few causes show up, something someone said, how you slept, something older than today, laid out like lenses on a bench.
Notice whether the feeling changes size as you look; if it doesn't, that's fine too.

wordCard.voice: Spinoza's calm: not a feeling switched off, but a feeling understood, its causes seen clearly, so it pushes you around a little less. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Spinoza's word in the Ethics for an emotion or feeling.

carryVoice: Your line: understand it. A feeling seen whole pushes a little less. That's day six hundred sixty-two.
